Become one in the bank account before you fracture over it. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and unify your wallet.

all.title: In-Laws and Boundaries: Leaving and Cleaving
all.excerpt: Genesis 2:24 commands a man to leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife. A new household needs new boundaries, not old loyalties.
content: Genesis 2:24 commands a man to leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife. Marriage forms a new household with its own headship, its own culture, and its own boundaries. Leaving is not abandoning; it is reordering loyalty so the new unit can stand.

When a spouse continues to run decisions through parents before the marriage, or a parent treats the married child as still under their roof, the cleaving never fully happens. Honoring parents (Exodus 20:12) does not mean obeying them after marriage. Setting respectful in-law boundaries is an act of love for the spouse and honor for the parents — it lets each relationship flourish in its proper lane.
Leave well, so you can cleave fully. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and build the boundary that protects the bond.

all.title: The Power of Spoken Blessings Over Your Marriage
all.excerpt: Proverbs 18:21 applies to the marriage bed: life and death are in the tongue. The words spouses speak over each other build or break the home.
content: Proverbs 18:21 applies directly to the bedroom: life and death are in the tongue, and the spouse's tongue is the closest one to your ear. The words you speak over your marriage — and over your spouse — are building materials, not just comments.

Speak blessings over your spouse daily: honor, vision, strength, favor. Replace 'you always' and 'you never' with 'I see the Lord on you' and 'I am grateful for you.' The atmosphere of a home is the sum of the words spoken inside it; a marriage bathed in spoken blessing becomes a greenhouse, not a courtroom.
Bless your spouse out loud, and watch the home warm. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and let your mouth build your marriage.

all.title: Forgiveness as a Covenant Discipline
all.excerpt: Forgiveness in marriage is not a feeling but a discipline. Ephesians 4:32 — forgive as God in Christ forgave you.
content: Forgiveness in marriage is not a warm feeling that arrives when the offense fades; it is a covenant discipline chosen while the wound is still sore. Ephesians 4:32 instructs, 'be kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake forgave you.'

Forgiveness is a decision to release the debt you have a right to collect. It does not deny the offense; it hands the ledger to God. In a long marriage, this discipline is repeated dozens of times — not because the offenses are small, but because the covenant is larger than any single wound. Unforgiveness builds a wall; forgiveness keeps the door open.
Forgive as a discipline, not as a mood. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and practice the discipline of release.

all.title: The Danger of Comparison: Social Media and the Neighbor's Marriage
all.excerpt: Comparing your raw, daily marriage to someone else's curated highlight reel is a slow poison. 2 Corinthians 10:12 says those who compare are unwise.
content: Comparing your raw, behind-the-scenes marriage to someone else's curated highlight reel is a slow poison. You see their vacation; you do not see their argument that preceded it. Second Corinthians 10:12 says those who measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves are without understanding.

Comparison breeds discontent with the spouse God gave you and envy of a marriage you do not actually know. The cure is gratitude for your own story and deliberate disengagement from content that fuels covetousness. Your marriage is not running behind anyone else's; it is running its own race, and comparison only makes you stumble in your lane.
Run your own lane, and delete the comparison. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and protect your marriage from the comparison trap.

all.title: Emotional Adultery: Guarding the Heart Against Micro-Infidelities
all.excerpt: Adultery begins in the heart long before the body. The 'harmless' confidant, the late-night chat, the inside joke — these are micro-infidelities that hollow the covenant.
content: Jesus said that looking lustfully is adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:28), and emotional adultery follows the same pattern. It begins with the 'harmless' confidant at work, the late-night chat, the inside joke that excludes the spouse. None of it crosses a physical line, yet all of it drains the covenant of its exclusivity.

Song of Solomon 4:12 describes the spouse as 'a locked garden, a sealed fountain.' The heart's intimacy is meant to flow only toward the spouse. Guarding against micro-infidelities means redirecting emotional energy home, shutting down confidants of the opposite sex, and refusing to make your spouse the only one who does not know your heart. Emotional exclusivity protects physical fidelity.
Seal the fountain; keep the garden locked. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and guard your heart from micro-infidelity.

all.title: The Role of Intimacy in Spiritual Warfare
all.excerpt: 1 Corinthians 7:5 — do not deprive one another, lest Satan tempt you. Marital intimacy is a frontline defense, not a private luxury.
content: First Corinthians 7:5 warns married couples not to deprive one another of physical intimacy, except by mutual agreement for a season of prayer, 'lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control.' Marital intimacy is not merely a private pleasure; it is a frontline defense in spiritual warfare.

The enemy exploits prolonged deprivation to sow temptation, distance, and eventually adultery. Regular, joyful marital intimacy is a weapon of protection as much as a gift of pleasure. Couples who treat intimacy as optional or negotiable leave a door open that the enemy is glad to walk through. The marriage bed is a shield, not a chore.
Defend the marriage with the intimacy God designed. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and wield intimacy as warfare.

all.title: Parenting in Unity: The Single Front of Discipline
all.excerpt: Children are experts at dividing parents. A united front — never contradicting each other in the child's presence — is the strength of the home.
content: Children are instinctive experts at finding the gap between parents and widening it. A united front — where parents never contradict or undermine each other in the child's presence — is the structural strength of the home. Division is the doorway a child learns to walk through.

Proverbs 22:6 instructs us to train a child in the way they should go, and training requires agreement. Disagree about discipline in private; present one decision in public. When children see that 'no' from one parent means 'no' from both, they gain security instead of leverage. The strength of the parenting is the unity of the parents.
Present one front, and the child gains a foundation. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and parent as a single wall, not two doors.

all.title: The Principle of Covering: Spiritual Headship and Protection
all.excerpt: 1 Corinthians 11:3 — the head of every man is Christ, the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God. Covering is order, not rank.
content: First Corinthians 11:3 establishes an order of covering: the head of every man is Christ, the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God. Covering is about order and protection, not rank and superiority — even Christ, equal with God, submitted to the Father.

Spiritual headship is the husband's responsibility to pray, protect, and provide spiritually for the home, standing as a shield between the family and the enemy. A wife under godly covering flourishes; a wife without it is exposed. The husband who refuses to cover has abandoned his post, and the wife who despises the covering has rejected her shield.
Cover your home, and be covered yourself. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and understand the protection of headship.

all.title: The Power of Praising Your Spouse in Public
all.excerpt: Proverbs 27:2 — let another praise you, not your own mouth. Public praise of your spouse builds their honor and announces your loyalty.
content: Proverbs 27:2 says, 'let another man praise you, and not your own mouth.' In marriage, this becomes a beautiful discipline: praising your spouse in public so that the world hears your loyalty before it hears your complaints. Public praise is a shield around your spouse's honor.

When you speak well of your spouse in gatherings — their character, their work, their parenting — you build their reputation, strengthen their confidence, and announce to all that this union is safe. The opposite, complaining about your spouse to friends, recruits allies against your own home. Praise in public, correct in private: that order protects both the person and the marriage.
Praise them where others can hear, and protect what you love. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and let your public words guard your private bond.

all.title: Listening to Understand, Not to Reply
all.excerpt: James 1:19 — be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger. Most marriage arguments end where true listening begins.
content: James 1:19 instructs us to be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. Most marriage arguments do not end with a solution; they end the moment one spouse truly feels heard. Listening to understand — rather than listening to formulate a reply — is a rare and healing skill.

When you listen to reply, you are defending your position while pretending to engage. When you listen to understand, you put down your argument long enough to actually receive your spouse's heart. Repeat back what you heard before you answer; you will be amazed how many 'arguments' were simply two people talking past each other.
Listen for the heart, not for the rebuttal. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and let understanding end your arguments.

all.title: The Discipline of Keeping Short Accounts
all.excerpt: Keeping short accounts means offenses are addressed quickly, not stockpiled. Unresolved hurts compound into walls no apology can later climb.
content: Keeping short accounts is the discipline of addressing offenses quickly rather than stockpiling them. Unresolved hurts do not evaporate; they accumulate, building invisible walls that no single apology can later climb. The debt grows interest in the wrong account.

Ephesians 4:26-27 warns not to let the sun go down on wrath, nor to give the enemy a foothold. A short-account marriage clears the ledger daily: 'I was hurt by what you said; can we talk about it?' The conversation is small; the cost of skipping it is enormous. Long accounts build cold houses; short accounts build warm ones.
Clear the ledger daily, and starve the enemy of a foothold. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and keep your accounts short.

all.title: The Place of Laughter and Joy in the Home
all.excerpt: Proverbs 17:22 — a merry heart does good like medicine. A home without laughter is sick even when nothing is wrong.
content: Proverbs 17:22 says, 'a merry heart does good like medicine.' Laughter is not a luxury in marriage; it is medicine. A home without laughter is quietly sick even when nothing is technically wrong. Joy is the immune system of the household.

Nehemiah 8:10 reminds us that the joy of the Lord is our strength. Cultivate shared humor, playful teasing, and unhurried delight in each other. Couples who laugh together weather conflict more lightly and forgive more quickly. Heaviness is not holiness; a joyful home is a strong home.
Laugh together often; it is medicine you can afford. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and let joy be the medicine of your home.

all.title: The Wisdom of Dating Your Spouse After Marriage
all.excerpt: The courtship that won the heart is the courtship that keeps it. Marriage is not the end of dating; it is the reason to keep dating.
content: The courtship that won the heart is the same courtship that keeps it. Marriage is not the finish line of dating; it is the reason to keep dating. What was done intentionally before the vows must be done intentionally after them.

Song of Solomon celebrates ongoing delight between the lovers, not a one-time conquest. Schedule regular time alone — walks, dinners, undistracted conversation. The spouse who feels pursued feels valued, and the marriage that keeps dating keeps its spark. Routine is the quiet enemy of romance; intentional dating is its steady defense.
Keep dating the one you married. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and let courtship outlast the wedding.

all.title: The Danger of Unspoken Expectations
all.excerpt: Unspoken expectations are premeditated resentments. Your spouse cannot meet a standard you never communicated.
content: Unspoken expectations are premeditated resentments. The moment you expect something you never asked for, you set your spouse up to fail a test they did not know they were taking. Disappointment becomes inevitable by design.

Proverbs 27:5 says, 'better is open rebuke than hidden love' — clarity is kinder than silence. A spouse cannot meet a standard they were never told about. Bring expectations into the open gently and early: about chores, finances, intimacy, holidays, family. The awkward conversation today prevents the silent resentment of next year.
Say what you hope for, and spare your spouse the guesswork. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and turn expectations into conversations.

all.title: Honoring Each Other's Strengths and Weaknesses
all.excerpt: Marriage joins two incomplete people. Honoring strengths and covering weaknesses — instead of exposing them — is the daily art of oneness.
content: Marriage joins two incomplete people, not two perfect ones. Each spouse brings strengths the other lacks and weaknesses the other must cover. The daily art of oneness is honoring the strengths and quietly covering the weaknesses rather than exposing them.

First Peter 4:8 says, 'above all, love one another deeply, because love covers a multitude of sins.' Do not broadcast your spouse's flaws; bear them. Do not compete with their strengths; celebrate them. A marriage that covers weaknesses and honors strengths becomes a team stronger than either partner alone.
Cover the weak spot; celebrate the strong one. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and learn the art of covering.

all.title: The Power of Praying Together
all.excerpt: Matthew 18:19 — if two of you agree on earth, it will be done. A couple that prays together invites God into the center of the union.
content: Matthew 18:19 promises that when two on earth agree about anything they ask, it will be done by the Father. A couple that prays together does more than share a spiritual habit — they invite God into the very center of their union, and the center holds.

Praying together softens hearts, aligns vision, and exposes hidden tensions before they harden. It is harder to stay angry with someone you have just held hands with in prayer. Couples who pray together daily build a shared spiritual floor that no storm can easily sweep away. The family that prays together is not a cliché; it is a fortress.
Pray together, and let God hold the center. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and build the habit that holds your home.

all.title: The Role of Gratitude in Sustaining Love
all.excerpt: 1 Thessalonians 5:18 — give thanks in all circumstances. Gratitude is the fertilizer that keeps love growing long after the honeymoon.
content: First Thessalonians 5:18 instructs us to give thanks in all circumstances. In marriage, gratitude is not a polite courtesy; it is the fertilizer that keeps love growing long after the honeymoon soil has settled. Entitlement withers what appreciation waters.

A spouse who is continually thanked for ordinary things — the meal, the laundry, the early morning, the patience — keeps giving. A spouse who is treated as though everything is owed stops giving. Gratitude trains the heart to see, and what is seen is cherished. The marriage that practices daily thankfulness never runs out of reasons to stay.
Water your love with gratitude, and it will not wither. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and let gratitude sustain your love.

all.title: The Discipline of Servant Leadership in the Home
all.excerpt: Mark 10:44 — whoever wants to be first must be servant of all. Biblical headship is servant leadership, not sovereign rule.
content: Mark 10:44 says, 'whoever wants to be first must be servant of all.' Biblical headship is servant leadership, not sovereign rule. The husband who leads is the husband who serves — washing dishes, listening, sacrificing preference, laying down his life.

Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the Church and gave Himself up for her. Christ's leadership was a cross, not a crown. A husband who leads by service earns the trust that makes his wife's submission a joy rather than a burden. Authority that serves is authority that is followed.
Lead by serving, and your authority will be followed. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and lead your home as a servant.

all.title: The Principle of Sowing Into Your Spouse's Vision
all.excerpt: A spouse's dream is part of the shared field. Sowing into your partner's vision — time, prayer, money, encouragement — is sowing into your own harvest.
content: Your spouse's dream is not a rival to your own; it is part of the shared field. Sowing into your partner's vision — with time, prayer, money, and encouragement — is not a distraction from your goals; it is a deposit into your shared harvest. Two visions became one at the altar.

Ecclesiastes 4:9 says two are better than one because they have a good reward for their labor. When a husband champions his wife's calling, or a wife prays her husband's business into being, the whole household rises. The spouse whose vision you water will, in season, water yours. Covenant vision is shared, not competed for.
Sow into their dream, and reap together. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and invest in your spouse's vision.

all.title: The Danger of Withholding Affirmation
all.excerpt: Withholding words of affirmation as punishment is a silent weapon that starves the very heart you promised to feed.
content: Withholding words of affirmation as a form of punishment is a silent weapon. The spouse who uses it may win a moment of control, but they are starving the very heart they promised to feed. Affirmation withheld is love rationed, and rationed love breeds resentment.

Proverbs 12:25 says, 'an anxious heart weighs a person down, but a kind word cheers it up.' Affirmation is daily bread, not a reward for performance. Speak it freely, especially when your spouse has failed, for that is when the bread is most needed. The marriage that starves its members of words cannot complain when they wither.
Feed your spouse with words, not silence. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and stop withholding the bread of affirmation.

all.title: The Wisdom of Maintaining Your Individual Identity
all.excerpt: Oneness is not sameness. Two whole people make one strong marriage; two fused, identity-less halves make a fragile one.
content: Oneness in marriage is not sameness. The 'one flesh' covenant joins two whole people; it does not erase them into two identity-less halves. Maintaining your individual identity — your gifts, friendships, and calling — is not a threat to the marriage; it is a strength of it.

First Corinthians 12 speaks of many members functioning as one body — distinct gifts, unified purpose. A spouse who dissolves into the other loses the very person the other married. Keep your friendships, your growth, your relationship with God, and your sense of self. Two whole people make one strong marriage; two empty halves make a fragile one.
Be whole, so your oneness is strong. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and keep your identity inside your covenant.

all.title: The Power of Small Acts of Kindness
all.excerpt: Grand gestures are rare; small daily kindnesses are constant. The marriage is built by a thousand tiny acts, not a few dramatic ones.
content: Grand romantic gestures are rare and memorable, but a marriage is not sustained by them. It is sustained by a thousand small daily kindnesses — the cup of water brought without asking, the door held, the burden carried for a tired moment. Love lives in the ordinary, not only the dramatic.

Galatians 6:2 says, 'bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.' Small kindnesses are the daily language of that bearing. The spouse who is served in small things trusts the spouse in large ones. A marriage built on consistent small kindnesses can survive almost any large crisis.
Build with small stones, and the house will stand. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and let small kindnesses build your love.

all.title: The Danger of Bringing Up Past Forgiven Sins
all.excerpt: Reopening a forgiven offense is a betrayal of the forgiveness you extended. God remembers our sins no more; marriage should imitate Him.
content: Reopening a forgiven offense is a quiet betrayal of the forgiveness you previously extended. When God forgives, He remembers our sins no more (Hebrews 8:12), and marriage is meant to imitate that divine amnesia. Dragging up the past turns forgiveness into a loan, not a gift.

Forgiveness that comes with an open file is not really forgiveness; it is leverage held in reserve. Once an offense is repented of and forgiven, it is buried — and buried things must not be exhumed to win arguments. The spouse who keeps bringing up the past cannot build a future, because they keep digging up the floor.
Bury it, and do not dig it up. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and let forgiven sins stay buried.

all.title: The Principle of 'Covering Each Other's Nakedness'
all.excerpt: Genesis 9 — Shem and Japheth walked backward to cover their father's nakedness. Marriage is the discipline of covering, not exposing, your spouse.
content: In Genesis 9, when Noah lay uncovered in his tent, his sons Shem and Japheth walked backward with a garment so that they would not see their father's nakedness, and they covered him. Ham, who looked and told, was cursed. The lesson is the principle of covering: the covenant partner covers, never exposes.

First Peter 4:8 says love covers a multitude of sins. Covering your spouse means protecting their vulnerabilities, their failings, and their exposed moments — from gossip, from in-laws, even from your own irritation. Exposing your spouse's weakness is the way of Ham, not of the covenant. The marriage that covers is the marriage that heals.
Walk backward and cover, never look and tell. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and learn to cover your spouse's nakedness.

all.title: The Role of Patience in Long-Term Love
all.excerpt: 1 Corinthians 13:4 — love is patient. Long-term love is built on enduring with a spouse through slow seasons of growth, not demanding instant change.
content: First Corinthians 13:4 begins its definition of love with one word: patient. Long-term love is not built on sudden romance but on enduring with a spouse through slow seasons of growth, immaturity, and change. Patience is not passivity; it is faith that the same God who is forming you is forming them.

Philippians 1:6 promises that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion — and the same is true for your spouse. Demanding instant maturity exhausts a marriage; patient endurance strengthens it. The spouse you married is becoming the spouse you will have; love walks with them through the becoming.
Be patient with their becoming, as God is with yours. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and let patience carry your love.

all.title: The Wisdom of Seeking Counsel Before Crisis
all.excerpt: Proverbs 15:22 — plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed. Seek counsel while the marriage is well, not only when it is breaking.
content: Proverbs 15:22 says, 'plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.' Most couples seek counsel only when the marriage is already breaking. The wiser path is to seek counsel while the marriage is well — building a relationship with mentors and a counselor before the crisis makes the difference.

Routine check-ins with a trusted mentor couple catch small cracks before they become fault lines. A marriage that has counsel on speedlist is a marriage that does not have to invent help in an emergency. The cost of periodic counsel is trivial next to the cost of a preventable collapse.
Build the counsel relationship before you need it. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and seek counsel before the crisis.

all.title: The Power of Celebrating Milestones Together
all.excerpt: Anniversaries, promotions, answered prayers — milestones are the memorials of a marriage. Celebrating them builds a shared story worth protecting.
content: Anniversaries, promotions, answered prayers, the child's first step — milestones are the memorials of a marriage. In Joshua 4, God had Israel set up stones so that future generations would ask, 'what do these mean?' Couples need their own stones: moments deliberately remembered so the story is not forgotten.

Celebrating milestones builds a shared narrative, a sense of 'look how far we have come' that sustains the marriage through the lean seasons. The couple that celebrates together remembers together, and remembrance is the fuel of gratitude. Do not let ordinary years pass unmarked; mark them, and the marriage gains a story worth protecting.
Set up stones, and tell your children what they mean. This is one of 500 nuggets in Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and celebrate the milestones of your love.

all.title: The Ultimate Goal: A Marriage That Preaches the Gospel
all.excerpt: Ephesians 5:31-32 — marriage is a profound mystery referring to Christ and the Church. Your marriage is a sermon the world reads without hearing a word.
content: Ephesians 5:31-32 reveals that marriage is a profound mystery referring to Christ and the Church. The ultimate goal of marriage is not merely the happiness of the spouses; it is the visible preaching of the gospel to a watching world. Your marriage is a sermon people read without ever hearing you speak.

When a husband loves his wife sacrificially, he shows the world how Christ loves the Church. When a wife honors her husband, she shows the world how the Church responds to Christ. Every act of forgiveness, every kept vow, every restored conflict is a verse in that sermon. The marriage that fails to preach Christ has missed its deepest purpose; the marriage that does becomes a living letter (2 Corinthians 3:2).
Preach the gospel with your marriage, not only with your mouth. This is the culminating lesson of Love Capsules — get the full book from the Library Store and let your marriage preach.

all.title: The Misunderstood Path: Marriage Is Not Mandatory for Everyone
all.excerpt: Matthew 19:11 corrects the assumption that everyone must marry. Marriage is a specific calling, not a universal requirement.
content: Society often presents marriage as a universal requirement — something every person must fulfill to be considered complete. Matthew 19:11 corrects this directly: 'Not everyone can accept this word, but only those to whom it has been given.' Marriage is a specific calling, not a universal rule.

Marriage requires particular resources, timing, and internal design. Pursuing it simply to conform to cultural pressure or family compulsion — without the grace or the mandate for it — leads to relational devastation. A wedding without a calling produces a household without a compass. Understanding where you fit in God's blueprint frees you to live a deliberate, focused life.
A fulfilled single is closer to destiny than a miserable married. This is the opening lesson of Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and count the tower before you lay the brick.

all.title: The Gift of Celibacy and the Single Mantle
all.excerpt: 1 Corinthians 7:7 names celibacy as a gift. Newton, Tesla, and others proved that extraordinary impact is possible outside marriage.
content: For certain individuals, living without romantic marriage is a specific, grace-filled gift from God. First Corinthians 7:7 says, 'I wish that all of you were as I am. But each of you has your own gift from God.' For those with this gift, solitude is not loneliness — it is a serene space to connect with the Creator and fulfill an assignment.

History proves the point. Sir Isaac Newton and Nikola Tesla both articulated a total lack of desire for marriage, dedicating their solitary lives to discoveries that transformed humanity. First Corinthians 7:32 notes that an unmarried person is concerned with the Lord's affairs without domestic division. Singleness, when embraced as a gift, concentrates focus rather than shrinking it.
Recognize your completeness in Christ. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and discover whether your gift is the ring or the room.

all.title: The Wisdom of Contentment in Singleness
all.excerpt: Philippians 4:11 — I have learned to be content whatever the circumstances. Singleness is a season to master contentment, not a problem to escape.
content: Philippians 4:11 records Paul's secret: 'I have learned to be content whatever the circumstances.' Singleness is not a problem to be escaped; it is a season to master contentment — the ability to be whole and joyful exactly where God has placed you.

The single who has not learned contentment will carry that same restlessness into marriage, where it will simply find new objects to crave. Contentment is not apathy; it is the settled trust that God's timing and portion are good. The single who is content today is the spouse who will be content tomorrow, because contentment travels with the person, not the status.
Master contentment now, and it will serve your marriage later. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and learn to be whole where you are.

all.title: The Principle of Readiness Over Age
all.excerpt: Age does not make you ready; character, capacity, and calling do. Marrying by a deadline is marrying by the wrong calendar.
content: The world measures readiness by age — 'I am thirty, I should be married.' Scripture measures readiness by character, capacity, and calling. A forty-year-old without self-mastery is not ready; a twenty-five-year-old with vision, discipline, and emotional health may be. The clock is the wrong calendar.

Luke 12:48 says, 'to whom much is given, much will be required.' Marriage requires the capacity to carry another person's life. Readiness is about whether you can bear the weight of a covenant, not whether you have reached a birthday. Marry when you are ready, not when you are rushed.
Ready is better than early. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and measure readiness by capacity, not age.

all.title: Financial Readiness Before Marriage
all.excerpt: 1 Timothy 5:8 — failing to provide for one's household is a denial of the faith. Financial readiness is a form of love, not materialism.
content: First Timothy 5:8 warns that failing to provide for one's own household is a denial of the faith. Financial readiness before marriage is a form of love, not materialism. Entering a covenant without the capacity to provide or manage resources responsibly places an avoidable weight on the very person you promised to care for.

Financial readiness does not mean wealth; it means a working plan, disciplined habits, and the willingness to carry economic weight. Love that refuses to prepare is love that plans to struggle. The romance that ignores the finances is building a house with no floor. Prepare your pocket before you propose.
Prepare your finances as an act of love. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and let readiness be your love language.

all.title: Emotional Readiness: The Heart That Can Hold
all.excerpt: Marriage requires a heart stable enough to hold another person's life without collapsing. Emotional readiness is the capacity to bear, not just to feel.
content: Marriage requires a heart stable enough to hold another person's life — their moods, dreams, wounds, and growth — without collapsing under the weight. Emotional readiness is not the intensity of your feelings; it is the capacity to bear, to regulate, and to remain present.

Proverbs 25:28 says a person without self-control is like a city broken down without walls. The emotionally unready spouse turns every disagreement into a crisis and every wound into a war. Emotional readiness is built before the altar: through healing, through discipline, through learning to sit with discomfort instead of fleeing it. A heart that cannot hold itself cannot hold another.
Build a heart that can hold before you ask one to hold you. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and prepare your emotional capacity.

all.title: Spiritual Readiness: Being Equally Yoked in Vision
all.excerpt: 2 Corinthians 6:14 — do not be unequally yoked. Spiritual readiness means both partners pull the same load in the same direction.
content: Second Corinthians 6:14 asks, 'what fellowship has light with darkness?' Spiritual readiness means that both partners are pulling the same load in the same direction — submitted to Christ, committed to His word, and walking toward a shared eternal goal.

Unequal yoking is not merely about denominational labels; it is about direction. One partner on fire for God and the other lukewarm produces a marriage that pulls in two directions and goes nowhere. Spiritual readiness means your private devotion, your church commitment, and your hunger for God are already established before you seek a spouse. A yoke works only when both animals walk the same way.
Walk the same direction before you share the yoke. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and check your spiritual readiness.

all.title: The Danger of Marrying Out of Pressure
all.excerpt: Pressure from family, peers, and age is a terrible matchmaker. A covenant made under duress is a covenant made without discernment.
content: Pressure is a terrible matchmaker. Whether it comes from family asking 'when will you marry,' from peers all getting engaged, or from the ticking of your own age — pressure forces decisions that discernment should have made. A covenant made under duress is a covenant made without vision.

Proverbs 29:25 says, 'fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the Lord is kept safe.' The pressure to conform is a snare that traps people in marriages they never prayerfully chose. The single who can withstand pressure is the single who can hear God. Wait for the green light of peace, not the red light of panic.
Refuse the pressure, and wait for peace. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and never marry under duress.

all.title: The Wisdom of Waiting for God's Best
all.excerpt: Isaiah 64:4 — God acts for the one who waits for Him. Waiting for God's best is not delay; it is the protection of your future.
content: Isaiah 64:4 celebrates a God 'who acts for the one who waits for Him.' Waiting for God's best is not passivity or delay; it is the active trust that His selection is better than your hurry. The 'good enough' partner accepted in impatience often becomes the 'too late' regret of a lifetime.

Lamentations 3:25 says, 'the Lord is good to those whose hope is in Him, to the one who seeks Him.' Waiting is not sitting; it is seeking, preparing, and trusting. The single who waits for God's best is not wasting time; they are protecting a future they cannot yet see. God's best is worth the wait, and the wait is worth the best.
Wait for His best, and avoid your regret. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and trust the timing of God's best.

all.title: The Role of Purpose Discovery Before Marriage
all.excerpt: Two halves do not make a whole; two whole people make one. Discover your purpose before you share a life — a spouse is meant to join a vision, not create it.
content: Two halves do not make a whole; two whole people make one. Genesis 1:27 shows God creating male and female as complete, image-bearing individuals. Purpose discovery before marriage means you enter the covenant as an asset with a vision, not as a needy consumer looking for someone to give your life meaning.

Habakkuk 2:2 instructs us to write the vision and make it plain. A spouse is meant to join a vision, not to be the source of it. The single who has not discovered purpose often expects marriage to provide it — and then resents the spouse for the emptiness that was always theirs to fill. Discover your purpose, and your marriage becomes a partnership of vision rather than a search for identity.
Find your purpose, then find your partner. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and discover your purpose before you propose.

all.title: The Principle of Healing Before Marriage
all.excerpt: Psalm 147:3 — God heals the brokenhearted. Unhealed wounds become the triggers of marriage. Heal before you cleave.
content: Psalm 147:3 promises that God heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. Unhealed emotional wounds do not vanish at the altar; they become the triggers of the marriage. The rejection, abandonment, or betrayal you carry in will eventually be projected onto the very person who came to love you.

Healing before marriage — through prayer, counsel, and sometimes therapy — is the gift you give your future spouse before you ever meet them. Your partner is not your therapist, and forcing them to pay for another person's knife is profoundly unfair. Heal before you cleave, so you bring health to the altar instead of a wound.
Heal now, and save your future spouse the bleeding. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and heal before you cleave.

all.title: The Danger of Marrying an Unhealed Person
all.excerpt: You cannot be the therapist your partner refused to hire. Marrying an unhealed person signs you up to pay for wounds you did not inflict.
content: Just as you must heal before marriage, you must also be wary of marrying an unhealed person. You cannot be the therapist your partner refused to hire. Marrying someone still bleeding from unhealed wounds signs you up to pay, daily, for injuries you did not inflict.

Proverbs 4:23 tells us to guard our heart with all diligence. An unhealed spouse will interpret your love through the lens of their past wounds — your patience as indifference, your silence as rejection, your success as threat. Love can help, but it cannot replace the healing only God and deliberate work can bring. Encourage them toward healing first; consider covenant after.
You cannot love someone into wholeness they refuse to pursue. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and guard against marrying unhealed wounds.

all.title: Vetting Character Over Charm
all.excerpt: Charm is the audition; character is the performance. Vet who a person is when no one is watching, not who they performed on the date.
content: Charm is the audition; character is the performance. Anyone can perform well on a date, but marriage is lived in the unwatched moments — the tired evening, the financial pressure, the disagreement. Vet who a person is when no one is watching, not who they performed when you were impressed.

Proverbs 31:30 warns that 'charm is deceptive, and beauty is fleeting; but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised.' Character is observed over time and across contexts: how they treat waiters, how they handle money, how they speak of their family, how they respond to delay. A short courtship sees the charm; a long courtship sees the character. Do not marry the audition.
Marry the performance, not the audition. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and vet character over charm.

all.title: The Principle of Friendship Before Romance
all.excerpt: Proverbs 17:17 — a friend loves at all times. Build friendship before romance; the couples who survive the dry seasons were friends first.
content: Proverbs 17:17 says, 'a friend loves at all times.' Building friendship before romance is the principle that protects the relationship when the romance inevitably dims. The couples who survive the dry seasons are the ones who were genuine friends before they were anything else.

Romance is the spark; friendship is the fuel. When the spark dims, friendship is what keeps the union connected through the dark. Build shared laughter, transparent communication, and mutual respect before the romance makes you compete. Marry your best friend, and you will never run out of conversation; marry only your lover, and you will run out of sparks.
Become friends before you become flames. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and let friendship precede romance.

all.title: The Role of Spiritual Community in Singleness
all.excerpt: Hebrews 10:25 — do not forsake the assembling of yourselves together. Singleness is not meant to be lived in isolation; community is your covering.
content: Hebrews 10:25 warns us not to forsake the assembling of ourselves together. Singleness was never designed to be lived in isolation; the spiritual community is the single's covering — providing accountability, friendship, mentorship, and protection.

Ecclesiastes 4:10 says, 'if one falls down, his friend can help him up.' A single disconnected from community is vulnerable to loneliness, deception, and poor decisions made in private. Invest in a local church, small group, and meaningful friendships. The community that surrounds you in singleness will be the community that supports you in marriage.
Do not walk singleness alone; let community be your covering. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and let the body hold you.

all.title: The Principle of Sexual Purity Before Marriage
all.excerpt: 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5 — this is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality. Purity is a deposit on the marriage itself.
content: First Thessalonians 4:3-5 states plainly, 'this is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality.' Sexual purity before marriage is not an outdated rule; it is a deposit on the marriage itself. Purity protects your courtship judgment from premature chemical bonding and reserves the full physical bond for after the covenant.

Hebrews 13:4 honors marriage by keeping the bed undefiled. The body that learns to wait is the body that can be trusted inside the covenant. Purity is hard, but it is kind — it keeps you from signing a covenant while chemically intoxicated. The discipline of purity before marriage becomes the discipline of faithfulness inside it.
Keep purity as a deposit on your future bond. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and steward purity before the covenant.

all.title: The Danger of 'Missionary Dating'
all.excerpt: 2 Corinthians 6:14 — what fellowship has light with darkness? Dating an unbeliever to convert them reverses God's order and risks your own drift.
content: 'Missionary dating' — dating an unbeliever in the hope of leading them to Christ — reverses God's order by placing romance ahead of spiritual agreement. Second Corinthians 6:14 asks what fellowship light has with darkness, and what a believer has in common with an unbeliever.

You cannot disciple someone into becoming your spouse; you can only marry someone who is already walking the same road. The risk is not only that they may never change — it is that you, drawn by affection, may be the one who drifts. Spiritual agreement must precede romantic attachment, not follow it. Convert before you court, or do not court at all.
Do not date as a missionary; date within the faith. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and refuse missionary dating.

all.title: The Wisdom of Courtship as Discovery
all.excerpt: Courtship is for discovery, not trial marriage. Living as spouses before the covenant blurs the very judgment you need to make.
content: Courtship is a discovery phase, not a trial marriage. Playing husband and wife before the covenant is signed — emotionally, physically, or financially — blurs the very judgment you most need to make. You cannot objectively evaluate a role you have already inhabited.

Proverbs 18:24 notes there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother, but friendship must precede fusion. Keep courtship intentionally lighter than marriage: ask the hard questions, observe the patterns, and reserve the full privileges of covenant for after the covenant. Discovery requires distance; trial marriage removes it.
Discover from a distance before you fuse up close. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and keep courtship a discovery.

all.title: The Power of Saying No to the Wrong Person
all.excerpt: Saying no to the wrong person is saying yes to the right one. The courage to decline a good-enough match protects the God-given one.
content: Saying no to the wrong person is, in effect, saying yes to the right one. The courage to decline a 'good enough' match — one that is convenient, available, or flattering but not God-given — protects the space for the one He has truly prepared. A 'no' to the wrong is a 'yes' to the right.

Matthew 7:6 warns not to give what is holy to dogs, nor pearls to pigs — a reminder that not every recipient is worthy of your covenant. The fear of being alone often drives people to accept the wrong person. But the single who can say no to the wrong has learned to trust God more than their fear. Keep the yes reserved; spend it only on the right.
Reserve your yes by spending your no wisely. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and learn the power of a holy no.

all.title: The Principle of Compatibility Over Chemistry
all.excerpt: Chemistry ignites; compatibility sustains. A marriage built on sparks alone burns out; one built on shared values endures.
content: Chemistry ignites; compatibility sustains. Chemistry is the spark that gets attention, but compatibility — shared values, vision, faith, finances, and conflict style — is the fuel that keeps the marriage running. A marriage built on sparks alone will burn out when the spark dims.

Amos 3:3 asks whether two can walk together unless they are agreed. Compatibility is not about being identical; it is about pulling in the same direction. The heart-racing chemistry of the first months will fade; the shared vision of a lifetime will not. Choose compatibility first, and let chemistry be the seasoning, not the main course.
Build on compatibility, and let chemistry season it. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and choose compatibility over chemistry.

all.title: The Danger of Ignoring Red Flags
all.excerpt: Red flags ignored in courtship become fault lines in marriage. A flag you rationalize away is a warning you will pay for later.
content: Red flags ignored in courtship do not disappear at the altar; they become fault lines in marriage. A pattern of dishonesty, a temper uncontrolled, a secret addiction, a disrespect for boundaries — these are warnings, not quirks to be patiently overcome. A flag you rationalize away is a warning you will pay for later.

Proverbs 22:3 says the prudent see danger and take refuge, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty. Infatuation is expert at painting red flags beige. Bring every concern into the light of trusted community and the counsel of mentors before you sign a covenant. It is kinder to break an engagement than to break a marriage.
Read the flags before you raise them down. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and refuse to ignore the red flags.

all.title: The Wisdom of Pre-Marital Counseling
all.excerpt: Proverbs 15:22 — with many advisers plans succeed. Premarital counseling belongs before engagement, not after regret.
content: Proverbs 15:22 says, 'plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.' Premarital counseling belongs before the engagement, not after the regrets. Too many couples seek counsel only after the wedding date is set, when pride and deposits make honest reconsideration nearly impossible.

A trained counselor surfaces the questions romance is too excited to ask — about finances, family, calling, conflict, and intimacy. The cost of a few sessions is infinitesimal next to the cost of a mismatched lifetime. Counsel while you can still walk away, and you will rarely have to walk away. The wisest couples are the ones who let wisdom interrupt their excitement.
Counsel while you can still cancel. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and let counsel precede your yes.

all.title: The Principle of Forgiveness Before Marriage
all.excerpt: Ephesians 4:32 — forgive as God forgave you. Unforgiveness toward your past is baggage you will unpack on your future spouse.
content: Ephesians 4:32 instructs us to forgive one another, even as God in Christ forgave us. Unforgiveness toward those who hurt you in your past is not left behind when you marry — it is baggage you will unpack on your future spouse, who will pay for wounds they did not cause.

Bitterness toward an ex, a parent, or a betrayer becomes the lens through which you interpret your spouse's every action. Forgiveness before marriage is not excusing the offender; it is releasing the debt so your heart is free to love again. The single who has not forgiven will bring a prisoner to the altar — and the prisoner may be themselves.
Forgive your past so it does not poison your future. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and forgive before you wed.

all.title: The Role of Mentors in the Decision to Marry
all.excerpt: Proverbs 11:14 — in a multitude of counselors there is safety. The decision to marry is too weighty to make in the echo chamber of two infatuated hearts.
content: Proverbs 11:14 says, 'where there is no counsel, the people fall; but in the multitude of counselors there is safety.' The decision to marry is too weighty to make in the echo chamber of two infatuated hearts. Mature mentors — married couples, pastors, parents — bring the sight your excitement has blinded.

A mentor asks the questions you are too in love to ask, observes patterns you have rationalized, and prays with a clarity your emotions have fogged. Their role is not to choose for you but to ensure you choose with both eyes open. The marriage built with counsel has a foundation the marriage built in private lacks.
Let mentors carry the weight of your decision. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and invite counsel into your choice.

all.title: The Principle of Vision Alignment Before Vows
all.excerpt: Proverbs 29:18 — without a vision the people perish. Two people with two different visions pull one marriage in two directions.
content: Proverbs 29:18 says, 'where there is no vision, the people perish.' Before vows are exchanged, a couple must verify that their visions are aligned — for career, for ministry, for family size, for location, for finances. Two people with two different visions will pull one marriage in two directions until something tears.

Amos 3:3 asks whether two can walk together unless they are agreed. Vision alignment does not mean identical dreams; it means a shared direction and a willingness to submit individual dreams to a common one. Negotiate the vision before the vows, not after. A wedding that unites two unaligned visions is a ceremony that signs a future conflict.
Align the vision before you sign the vows. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and align your vision first.

all.title: The Danger of Unequal Yoking
all.excerpt: 2 Corinthians 6:14 — do not be unequally yoked. A yoke works only when both animals are the same kind, walking the same way.
content: Second Corinthians 6:14 commands, 'do not be unequally yoked together with unbelievers.' The agricultural image is precise: a yoke joins two animals to pull together, but if they are of different size, strength, or direction, the yoke chafes, the work stalls, and both animals are injured.

Unequal yoking is broader than belief alone — it includes unequal commitment, unequal maturity, unequal vision, and unequal devotion. A marriage is a lifelong yoke; the slightest misalignment becomes a constant strain over decades. Marry someone of the same kind, walking the same way, pulling the same load. The wrong yoke turns partnership into pain.
Match the yoke to the animal, or both will be injured. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and refuse the unequal yoke.

all.title: The Wisdom of Counting the Cost
all.excerpt: Luke 14:28 — which of you, intending to build a tower, does not sit down first and count the cost? Marriage is a tower; count before you build.
content: Luke 14:28 asks, 'which of you, intending to build a tower, does not sit down first and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?' Marriage is a tower, and the wisdom of counting the cost before building is what prevents a half-finished, exposed structure.

Counting the cost means honestly assessing the sacrifice ahead — the death of independence, the financial weight, the emotional labor, the in-laws, the children, the lifelong commitment. The one who counts and still says yes builds with intention; the one who never counts builds with illusion. Marriage is not a leap of blind faith but a step of counted cost.
Count the cost, then build with both eyes open. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and count the cost of your tower.

all.title: Self-Discovery as the Narrow Path to Destiny
all.excerpt: Matthew 7:13-14 — enter through the narrow gate. Self-discovery is the green light that shows what to embrace and what to reject.
content: Matthew 7:13-14 commands us to enter through the narrow gate that leads to life. Self-discovery is the ultimate green light — it illuminates your true scope, helping you recognize what to embrace and what to reject. The narrow path is not crowded, but it is clear.

Understanding who you are in God, discovering your unique wiring, and mastering self-discipline moves you away from blind, panicked rushing and toward a calculated, purposeful walk. Two halves do not make a whole; two whole people make one. Discover your personal purpose and value before marriage, and you enter as an asset rather than a needy consumer.
Walk the narrow path of knowing yourself under God. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and step onto the narrow path to your destiny.

all.title: The Cost of Marrying to Escape
all.excerpt: Marrying to escape a present pain guarantees a worse, permanent one. A covenant built on exit is a covenant that cannot hold.
content: Marrying to escape a present pain — a difficult home, a dry season, a sense of falling behind — trades one temporary discomfort for a permanent commitment built on the wrong foundation. A covenant constructed as an exit door cannot hold when the escapist motive fades and the same emptiness resurfaces inside the new house.

Psalm 68:6 says God sets the lonely in families, and His remedy for loneliness is first Himself, then healthy community, and only then marriage in its proper season. The marriage that began as an escape becomes, in time, a cage the person cannot leave. Deal with the pain at its root before you drag another person into it. Marriages built to exit a room rarely become homes.
Don't marry to escape a room; marry to build a home. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and refuse to marry as an exit.

all.title: Marriage Is Not a Hospital: Get Fixed Before You Seek a Spouse
all.excerpt: Psalm 147:3 says God heals the brokenhearted. Marriage is a synergy arena, not a psychological ward. Bring health to the altar.
content: Psalm 147:3 promises that God heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. Marriage, however, is a functional arena of synergy — not a psychological hospital. Forcing a partner to pay the full price for emotional damage inflicted by someone else is profoundly unfair.

Unhealed wounds make you interpret innocent mistakes as deliberate attacks. You bleed on the people who did not cut you. If you are still bleeding from past betrayals, seek therapy, prayer, and personal healing before you seek a spouse. Your partner is not your therapist and not the author of your pain. Get fixed first, so you bring health to the altar instead of a wound.
A whole person blesses a marriage; a bleeding one burdens it. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and bring health, not history, into your covenant.

all.title: The Wisdom of Building Yourself Before Building a Marriage
all.excerpt: Singleness is the construction season, not the waiting room. Build your character, skills, and faith now, so your marriage is built on a finished person.
content: Singleness is not a waiting room; it is a construction season. The character, skills, financial habits, and spiritual disciplines you build now become the foundation your marriage will stand on. A marriage built on an unfinished person is a house built on wet concrete.

Proverbs 24:27 says, 'prepare your outside work, make it fit for yourself in the field; and afterward build your house.' Build the field before you build the house. Use your singleness to study, save, heal, grow, and deepen your walk with God. The single who builds well marries as an asset; the single who merely waits marries as a project.
Build yourself first, so your marriage stands on a finished foundation. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and build during the construction season.

all.title: The Principle of Servant Readiness
all.excerpt: Mark 10:44 — whoever wants to be first must be servant of all. Marriage readiness is servant readiness: the willingness to lay down your life, daily, for another.
content: Mark 10:44 says, 'whoever wants to be first must be servant of all.' Marriage readiness is, at its core, servant readiness — the willingness to lay down your preferences, your time, and even your life, daily, for another person. The one who marries to be served is not ready to be married.

Philippians 2:3-4 instructs us to do nothing out of selfish ambition, but in humility to count others more significant than ourselves. The single who has not learned to serve — in church, in family, in friendships — will not suddenly learn it at the altar. Servant readiness is proven in small surrenders long before the vows. The heart that serves is the heart ready to marry.
Be a servant first, and your marriage will be ready. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and prepare your servant heart.

all.title: The Danger of Marrying an Unsubmitted Person
all.excerpt: A person who cannot submit to God, to counsel, or to spiritual authority cannot be safely led or safely followed in marriage.
content: A person who cannot submit to God, to wise counsel, or to spiritual authority cannot be safely led or safely followed in marriage. Submission to God is the prerequisite for healthy submission in marriage; the one accountable to no one is dangerous to everyone.

Hebrews 13:17 instructs us to obey our leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over our souls. An unsubmitted partner — untouchable, uncorrectable, accountable to no one — will bring that same untouchable spirit into the home. The spouse who cannot be spoken to cannot be partnered with. Watch how a person responds to authority before you bind yourself to them.
Marry someone accountable, or you will be married to a tyrant. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and beware the unsubmitted heart.

all.title: Purity as a Wedding Gift
all.excerpt: Sexual purity is not just a rule to keep; it is a gift to present. The undefiled marriage bed is a present few couples still bring to the altar.
content: Sexual purity is not merely a rule to keep; it is a gift to present. Hebrews 13:4 honors marriage by keeping the bed undefiled, and the undefiled marriage bed is a present few couples still bring to one another at the altar. Purity is the wrapping on the most intimate gift you will ever give.

First Corinthians 6:18 commands us to flee sexual immorality. The body that has been kept is a gift that can be given whole; the body that has been scattered has to be redeemed and then given. Grace covers every past failure, but the wisdom of purity guards a future gift that no second-hand experience can replicate. Present purity as a wedding gift, and let the marriage bed begin undefiled.
Wrap your wedding gift in purity. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and present purity at the altar.

all.title: The Wisdom of Dating With Intentionality
all.excerpt: Intentional dating asks 'could this lead to covenant?' Casual dating trains the heart to consume and discard; intentional dating trains it to evaluate and commit.
content: Intentional dating approaches every relationship with a clear question: 'could this, prayerfully, lead to covenant?' Casual dating — entertaining attention with no direction — trains the heart to consume and discard, rehearsing patterns that will sabotage a future marriage. Intentional dating trains the heart to evaluate and commit.

Proverbs 4:26 says, 'ponder the path of your feet, and let all your ways be established.' Do not entertain relationships that have no destination, and do not prolong connections you have already discerned are wrong. Intentionality protects both your heart and theirs. Date with purpose, or you will marry your patterns.
Date with a destination, not just a distraction. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and date with intentionality.

all.title: The Danger of Compromising Your Standards
all.excerpt: Standards lowered for the sake of availability become regrets paid for over a lifetime. The standard you compromise in courtship is the standard you live without in marriage.
content: Standards lowered for the sake of availability become regrets paid for over a lifetime. The core standards you hold — spiritual maturity, character, faithfulness, vision — are not preferences to be bargained away in loneliness. The standard you compromise in courtship is the standard you will live without for the rest of your marriage.

Psalm 16:6 says, 'the boundary lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; surely I have a delightful inheritance.' God-given standards are boundaries that protect your inheritance, not walls that block your happiness. Hold them gently but firmly, and trust that the One who set them will also send the one who meets them. A compromised standard is a door you cannot later close.
Hold the standard, and trust God for the match. This is one of 40 lessons in Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and refuse to compromise your standards.

all.title: Patience and Trusting God's Timing
all.excerpt: Ecclesiastes 3:11 — God has made everything beautiful in its time. Patience in the waiting season is not wasted; it is the preparation of a beautiful 'in its time.'
content: Ecclesiastes 3:11 says, 'He has made everything beautiful in its time.' Patience in the waiting season is not wasted time; it is the unseen preparation that makes the 'in its time' beautiful. God's timing is never late, even when it feels slow to a heart that is tired of waiting.

Isaiah 30:18 promises, 'blessed are all those who wait for Him.' The waiting season is where God forms the character, contentment, and capacity that the marriage will need. The single who waits well arrives at the altar whole; the single who rushes arrives fractured. Trust the One who writes the story, and let Him finish the chapter before you turn the page.
Wait well, and arrive whole. This is the final lesson of Don't Marry — get the full book from the Library Store and trust the beauty of God's timing.
